En 1642, un jeune homme de 19 ans fait a: In 1642, a 19-year-old makes toothed wheels add up to help his father count taxes.
Blaise Pascal commence sa machine en 164: Blaise Pascal starts his machine in 1642, at 19, to ease the calculations of his father, in charge of taxes in Rouen. He presents it in 1645.
Chaque roue porte les chiffres 0 à 9 ; q: Each wheel carries the digits 0 to 9; when a wheel goes from 9 to 0, a part, the jumper, drops under its own weight and moves the next wheel on one notch: that is the carry.
La machine ne sait qu'additionner. Pour: The machine can only add. To subtract, you add the nines' complement of the number.
Pascal fait une cinquantaine de prototyp: Pascal makes some fifty prototypes; about twenty machines are built and nine still exist.
La Pascaline n'est pas la toute première: The Pascaline is not the very first calculating machine described: in 1623, Wilhelm Schickard draws a "calculating clock". But it is the first one produced in several copies and preserved.
+1 aux unités : 099 devient 100, la rete: +1 to the units: 099 becomes 100, the carry drops from wheel to wheel
La Pascaline : trois roues 0, 9, 9 ; ajo: The Pascaline: three wheels 0, 9, 9; adding 1 passes the carry from the units to the tens, then to the hundreds
Leibniz fait multiplier une machine par: Leibniz makes a machine multiply by repeated additions, and dreams of writing every number with only 0 and 1.
En 1673, Leibniz présente à la Royal Soc: In 1673, Leibniz presents to the Royal Society in London the wooden model of a machine that multiplies and divides, as well as adding and subtracting.
Son cœur est le cylindre cannelé, ou rou: Its heart is the stepped drum, or Leibniz wheel: teeth of different lengths. It was used in mechanical calculators down to the Curta, in the 1970s.
En binaire, chaque position vaut le doub: In binary, each position is worth twice its right-hand neighbour: 1, 2, 4, 8… So 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.
Leibniz écrit sur le binaire dès 1679, m: Leibniz writes about binary as early as 1679, but publishes his "Explanation of Binary Arithmetic" in 1705, after receiving the Chinese hexagrams of the Yi Jing from the Jesuit Bouvet.
Leibniz n'a pas construit de machine bin: Leibniz did not build a binary machine: his calculating machine works in base 10. Binary only enters machines in the 20th century.
Chaque case vaut le double de sa voisine: Each box is worth twice its right-hand neighbour
Un métier à tisser lyonnais lit son moti: A Lyon loom reads its pattern from holed cards: the first program you can change without touching the machine.
Joseph Marie Jacquard présente son mécan: Joseph Marie Jacquard presents his mechanism at the Exhibition of Year IX, in Paris, in 1801, and patents it on December 23, 1801.
Il remplace le « tireur de lacs », l'ouv: It replaces the "draw boy", the worker who lifted the threads of the pattern by hand.
Les cartes, reliées en chaîne, passent d: The cards, linked in a chain, pass in front of needles: where there is a hole, the needle goes through and lifts its thread; otherwise the thread stays down.
Changer de motif, c'est changer de carte: Changing the pattern means changing the cards: the machine stays the same. Babbage will take up this idea to control his Analytical Engine.
Jacquard n'a pas tout inventé seul : il: Jacquard did not invent everything alone: in particular, he rebuilt a loom designed by Vaucanson in the mid-18th century. His stroke of genius was to make it a reliable, widespread mechanism.
Un trou : l'aiguille passe et lève son f: A hole: the needle goes through and lifts its thread
Pas de trou : le fil reste en bas: No hole: the thread stays down
Carte perforée de Jacquard : chaque trou: Jacquard punched card: each hole lets through a needle that lifts a warp thread
Babbage, le moulin et le magasin: Babbage, the mill and the store
En 1837, Charles Babbage dessine une mac: In 1837, Charles Babbage designs a machine that separates calculation from memory. No one will build it.
Après sa machine à différences, conçue d: After his Difference Engine, designed in the 1820s, Babbage describes his Analytical Engine in 1837.
Le « moulin » fait les quatre opérations: The "mill" does the four operations and comparisons: it is the ancestor of the arithmetic unit, the ALU.
Le « magasin » devait garder 1 000 nombr: The "store" was to hold 1,000 numbers of 40 digits: it is the ancestor of memory.
Des cartes perforées, comme celles des m: Punched cards, like those of Jacquard looms, give the orders. The machine provides for conditional branching and loops.
La machine analytique n'a jamais été con: The Analytical Engine was never built. His son Henry built a small part of the mill between 1880 and 1910; it is at the Science Museum in London.
Machine analytique de Babbage : le magas: Babbage's Analytical Engine: the store keeps the numbers, the mill calculates, the punched cards give the orders
En traduisant un article sur la machine: Translating an article on Babbage's engine, Ada Lovelace writes notes three times longer, including a real program.
En 1843, Ada Lovelace traduit en anglais: In 1843, Ada Lovelace translates into English the Italian Menabrea's article on the Analytical Engine, and adds her notes, signed A.A.L.
Ses notes sont trois fois plus longues q: Her notes are three times longer than the article itself.
La note G détaille, opération par opérat: Note G sets out, operation by operation, how the engine would calculate a Bernoulli number: it is often presented as the first published program.
Un algorithme est une suite d'instructio: An algorithm is a sequence of precise instructions; a loop repeats a group of instructions until a test is satisfied.
Le programme de la note G contient une e: The program in note G contains an error: in operation 4, a division is written upside down. No one saw it in her lifetime, since the engine was never built.
Un algorithme avec une boucle : on calcu: An algorithm with a loop: calculate, test whether it is done, otherwise start again
En 1937, un étudiant du MIT montre que d: In 1937, an MIT student shows that switches can do Boolean logic, and therefore calculation.
En 1937, au MIT, Claude Shannon écrit so: In 1937, at MIT, Claude Shannon writes his master's thesis, "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits", published in 1938.
Il montre que l'algèbre de Boole sert à: He shows that Boolean algebra can be used to design and simplify the relay circuits of telephone exchanges.
Deux interrupteurs en série forment un E: Two switches in series form an AND: current only flows if both are closed. In parallel, they form an OR.
Le psychologue Howard Gardner l'a qualif: The psychologist Howard Gardner called it "possibly the most important, and also the most famous, master's thesis of the century".
Shannon n'a pas inventé l'algèbre de Boo: Shannon did not invent Boolean algebra, which dates from 1854: he applied it to electrical circuits.
La lampe s'allume si A et B / si A ou B: The lamp lights if A and B / if A or B are closed
Deux interrupteurs en série forment un E: Two switches in series form an AND, in parallel an OR
Ranger le programme dans la mémoire, com: Store the program in memory, like the data: the idea that turns a calculator into a computer.
Dans une machine à programme enregistré,: In a stored-program machine, the instructions are read from the same electronic memory as the data.
L'idée remonte à la machine universelle: The idea goes back to Turing's theoretical universal machine, in 1936.
En juin 1945, John von Neumann la décrit: In June 1945, John von Neumann describes it for the EDVAC in his "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC".
Le 21 juin 1948, à Manchester, la « Baby: On June 21, 1948, in Manchester, the "Baby" of Williams, Kilburn and Tootill runs a stored program for the first time: it looks for the largest divisor of a number.
L'architecture dite « de von Neumann » n: The so-called "von Neumann" architecture is not his alone: his report takes up ideas discussed with the ENIAC team, but only his name appears on it, not those of Eckert and Mauchly.
Programme et données dans la même mémoir: Program and data in the same memory
Programme enregistré : les instructions: Stored program: instructions and data are kept in the same memory, read by the processor
Grace Hopper, le bug et le compilateur: Grace Hopper, the bug and the compiler
Une mathématicienne de la marine américa: A US Navy mathematician teaches computers to read words, and makes a moth famous.
Grace Hopper (1906-1992) commence à prog: Grace Hopper (1906-1992) starts programming in 1944 on the Harvard Mark I, in Howard Aiken's team.
Le 9 septembre 1947, un papillon de nuit: On September 9, 1947, a moth is found stuck in a relay of the Mark II; it is taped into the logbook: "First actual case of bug being found".
En 1952, elle termine le système A-0, l': In 1952, she completes the A-0 system, one of the first compilers: a program that translates a program into machine instructions.
Ses travaux sur FLOW-MATIC inspirent le: Her work on FLOW-MATIC inspires the COBOL language, defined in 1959.
Le papillon n'a pas inventé le mot « bug: The moth did not invent the word "bug": Edison already used it in 1878 for small faults. The logbook says "first actual case" precisely because the word existed.
Il traduit, une fois pour toutes, avant: It translates once and for all, before the machine calculates
Un compilateur traduit un programme écri: A compiler translates a program written for humans into machine instructions
